en: The Shorter Exposition:
The Exposition of the Chapter on the Way to the Far Shore;
The Exposition of the Questions.
4. The Exposition of the Questions of the Youth Mettagū I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this—
thus spoke the Venerable Mettagū.
I consider you one who has reached the end of knowledge and developed the self;
from where indeed have these various forms of suffering in the world arisen?
“I ask you, Blessed One, tell me. Regarding “I ask”:
there are three kinds of questions—the question for the illumination of what has not been seen, the question for the confirmation of what has been seen, and the question for the cutting off of doubt.
What is a question for the purpose of illuminating what has not been seen?
It is when the characteristic of a thing is by nature unknown, unseen, unmeasured, unexamined, unmanifested, and unclarified.
One asks a question for the sake of its knowledge, for its seeing, for its measuring, for its examination, for the purpose of its manifestation, and for the purpose of its clarification.
This is a question for the purpose of revealing what has not been seen.
What is a question for the purpose of correlating what has been seen?
It is when the characteristic is known by nature—seen, weighed, judged, made manifest, and fully clarified.
He asks a question for the purpose of exchanging views with other wise people—
this is a question for the purpose of exchanging what has been seen.
What is a question for the purpose of cutting through doubt?
By nature he is prone to doubt, prone to perplexity, and full of uncertainty, thinking:
"Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it? He asks a question for the purpose of cutting through that doubt.
This is the question for cutting through doubt.
These are the three questions.
There are another three questions:
Questions by humans, questions by non-humans, and questions by created beings.
What are questions by humans?
Humans approach the Buddha, the Blessed One, and ask a question; monks ask; nuns [ask].
Laymen ask, laywomen ask, kings ask, kshatriyas ask, brahmins ask,
vaishyas ask, shudras ask, householders ask, and those who have gone forth ask—
this is questioning by humans.
What is the question of non-human beings? Non-human beings approach the Buddha, the Blessed One, and ask a question;
nāgas ask, supaṇṇas ask, yakkhas ask, asuras ask, gandhabbas ask, and the Great Kings ask.
Indra asks, Brahmā asks, the gods ask—
this is a question by non-humans.
What is a question by a created being?
The Blessed One creates a mind-made form, complete in all its limbs and parts, with no faculties lacking.
That created being approaches the Buddha, the Blessed One, and asks a question;
the Blessed One answers it.
This is the question regarding what is created.
These are the three questions.
There are another three questions as well:
A question about one’s own welfare, a question about the welfare of others, a question about the welfare of both … [and so on] … another three questions:
a question about welfare pertaining to the present life, a question about welfare pertaining to future lives, a question about ultimate welfare … another three questions:
A question concerning blamelessness, a question concerning the absence of defilement, a question concerning purification… another three questions:
a question concerning the past, a question concerning the future, a question concerning the present… another three questions:
a question concerning the internal, a question concerning the external, a question concerning both the internal and the external… another three questions:
A question on the wholesome, a question on the unwholesome, a question on the indeterminate… another three questions:
a question on the aggregates, a question on the elements, a question on the sense bases… another three questions:
a question on the foundations of mindfulness, a question on the right efforts, a question on the bases of psychic power… another three questions:
The inquiry into the faculties, the inquiry into the powers, the inquiry into the factors of enlightenment... and another three inquiries:
the inquiry into the path, the inquiry into the fruit, and the inquiry into Nibbāna...
"I ask you" means: I ask you, I entreat you, I beseech you, I inspire confidence in you; "please tell it to me"—thus I ask you.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for reverence... [and so on] ...it is a realization-designation, namely "Bhagavā.
"Tell me" means: speak, declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain, and explain.
"I ask you, Blessed One, please tell me this.
Thus spoke the Venerable Mettagū; "thus" (*iccā*) is the grammatical connection of the words... [etc.
...thus spoke the Venerable Mettagū.
"I consider you a master of knowledge (vedagu) with a developed mind.
I consider you a master of knowledge; I consider you one with a developed mind. Thus I know, thus I understand, thus I acknowledge, thus I penetrate.
How is the Blessed One a master of knowledge? A master of knowledge with a developed mind. And how is the Blessed One a master of knowledge?
"Veda" refers to the knowledge, wisdom, faculty of wisdom, and power of wisdom within the four paths;
it is the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor, inquiry, insight, and right view.
By means of these knowledges, the Blessed One has reached the end of birth, aging, and death; he has attained the end, reached the limit, attained the limit, and reached the boundary.
He has reached the limit, attained cessation, attained rest; he has reached shelter, attained shelter, reached a refuge, attained a refuge;
he has reached fearlessness, attained fearlessness, reached the deathless, attained the deathless, reached the immortal, attained the immortal, reached Nibbāna, attained Nibbāna.
One who has reached the end of the Vedas is a *vedagu*;
one who has reached the end by means of the Vedas is a *vedagu*;
or, because of having known the seven principles (*dhamma*), one is a *vedagu*.
The view of a personal body is understood; doubt is understood; adherence to rules and observances is understood;

lust, hatred, delusion, and conceit are understood. He has understood those evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and conducive to future birth, aging, and death.
"Having scrutinized all the Vedas,
O Sabhiya," said the Blessed One,
"and whatever [teachings] there are among the recluses and the brahmins;"
"One who is free from passion toward all feelings,
having transcended all feeling— he is a Vedagū.
Thus was the Blessed One a Vedagū.
In what way is the Blessed One one whose self is developed?

The Blessed One has developed the body, developed virtue, developed the mind, developed wisdom; he has developed the foundations of mindfulness, developed the right efforts, developed the bases of psychic power, developed the faculties, developed the powers, developed the factors of enlightenment, and developed the path; he is one who has abandoned the defilements.
He has penetrated the unshakeable, realized cessation.
Suffering has been fully understood by him, its origin abandoned, the path developed, and cessation realized. That which is to be directly known has been directly known;

that which is to be fully understood has been fully understood; that which is to be abandoned has been abandoned; that which is to be developed has been developed; and that which is to be realized has been realized.
It has been realized: it is not limited, but vast, deep, immeasurable, unfathomable, and like the ocean with its many treasures.
It is endowed with the sixfold equanimity.
Having seen a form with the eye, one is neither glad nor sad.
He dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.

Having heard a sound with the ear, smelled an odor with the nose, tasted a flavor with the tongue, touched a tangible object with the body, or cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither glad nor sad;
he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
Having seen a form with the eye, he does not crave a pleasing form, does not become infatuated with it, and does not give rise to lust.
His body remains steady, his mind remains steady—well-composed and well-liberated within.
Furthermore, having seen a displeasing form with the eye, he is not dejected; his mind is not unsettled, his heart is not cowed, and his consciousness is not corrupted.
His body remains steady, and his mind remains steady within, well-composed and well-liberated.
Having heard a sound with the ear...

having smelled an odor with the nose... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... having felt a tangible object with the body... having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not crave it, does not become infatuated with it, and does not give rise to lust.
His body remains steady, and his mind remains steady, well-composed and well-liberated within.
When he cognizes a mental phenomenon with the mind that is disagreeable, he does not become dejected.
With a mind that is unestablished, a mind that is undepressed, and a mind that is free from ill will, his body remains steady, and his mind remains steady, well-composed and well-liberated within.
Having seen a form with the eye, the body remains steady and the mind remains steady amidst forms that are pleasing and displeasing; it is well-composed and well-liberated within.
Having heard a sound with the ear...

[and so on] ...having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, the body remains steady and the mind remains steady amidst phenomena that are pleasing and displeasing; it is well-composed and well-liberated within.

Having seen a form with the eye, one is not excited by what is provocative of lust, does not feel aversion toward what is provocative of hatred, is not deluded by what is provocative of delusion, is not agitated by what is provocative of anger, does not become intoxicated by what is provocative of pride, and is not defiled by what is provocative of the defilements.
Having heard a sound with the ear … [and so on] … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,

one is not excited by what is provocative of lust, does not feel aversion toward what is provocative of hatred, is not deluded by what is provocative of delusion, is not agitated by what is provocative of anger, does not become intoxicated by what is provocative of pride, and is not defiled by what is provocative of the defilements.
In what is seen, he is merely one who has seen; in what is heard, he is merely one who has heard; in what is sensed, he is merely one who has sensed;
in what is cognized, he is merely one who has cognized. He is not stained by what is seen, not stained by what is heard, not stained by what is sensed, and not stained by what is cognized.
Regarding what is seen, he dwells uninvolved, undepressed, independent, unbound, liberated, dissociated, with a mind free from the boundaries of the world.

In what is heard … in what is sensed … in what is cognized, he dwells unattached, unrepelled, independent, unbound, liberated, and dissociated, with a mind free from the boundaries of the conceptual world.
The Blessed One possesses the eye; the Blessed One sees forms with the eye; yet in the Blessed One there is no desire or lust; the Blessed One is well-liberated in mind.
The Blessed One possesses the ear; the Blessed One hears sounds with the ear; yet in the Blessed One there is no desire or lust;
the Blessed One is well-liberated in mind. The Blessed One possesses the nose; the Blessed One smells odors with the nose; yet in the Blessed One there is no desire or lust;

the Blessed One is well-liberated in mind. The Blessed One possesses the tongue; the Blessed One tastes flavors with the tongue; yet in the Blessed One there is no desire or lust; the Blessed One is well-liberated in mind.

The body of the Blessed One exists; the Blessed One touches tangible objects with his body; yet in the Blessed One there is no desire or lust; the Blessed One is well-liberated in mind. The mind of the Blessed One exists;
the Blessed One cognizes mental phenomena with his mind; yet in the Blessed One there is no desire or lust; the Blessed One is well-liberated in mind.
The eye delights in forms, rejoices in forms, and is gladdened by forms; but that [eye] of the Blessed One is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained.
And he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint.
The ear delights in sounds, is fond of sounds...

the nose delights in odors, is fond of odors... the tongue delights in flavors, is fond of flavors, and rejoices in flavors; yet that [tongue] of the Blessed One is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained.
And he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint:

the body delights in tangibles, rejoices in tangibles, and finds delight in tangibles... the mind delights in mental phenomena, rejoices in mental phenomena, and finds delight in mental phenomena; yet that Blessed One is tamed, guarded, protected, and restrained, and he teaches the Dhamma for its restraint.
“The tamed one they lead to the assembly;
the tamed one the king mounts.
The tamed one is the best among human beings.”
He endures harsh speech.
Better are the tamed mules, and the noble Sindhu horses; [but better still is the person who endures abuse].
And even great elephants, those noble tuskers—
yet one who has tamed themselves is better than these vehicles.
For indeed, by means of these vehicles, [one does not reach the goal].
One may go to a region never before reached;
for one who is self-tamed goes as one who is tamed by the tamed.
They do not waver amidst the various conditions,
being fully liberated from renewed existence;
they have reached the stage of the tamed.
They are victors in the world—
those whose faculties have been cultivated both internally and externally throughout the entire world.
“Having become disenchanted with this world and the world beyond,
he, being cultivated and tamed, awaits his time.
Thus, O Blessed One, I consider you one who has cultivated himself, a master of knowledge whose self is cultivated.
“From where, indeed, have these sufferings arisen?

Here, “from where, indeed” is a question of doubt, a question of perplexity, a question of ambiguity, a question of uncertainty—a question such as: “Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it?”
From what [does it arise]?
"Suffering": the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair;
the suffering of hell, the suffering of the animal realm, the suffering of the sphere of hungry ghosts, and the suffering of human beings.
Suffering rooted in descent into the womb; suffering rooted in remaining in the womb;
suffering rooted in emerging from the womb; suffering connected to one who is born; suffering pertaining to one who is born; suffering due to one's own initiative;
suffering due to the initiative of others; the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkha*); the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkha*); the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*); and eye disease.
Disease of the ear, disease of the nose, disease of the tongue, disease of the body, disease of the head, disease of the ear, disease of the mouth, disease of the teeth,
cough, asthma, catarrh, burning sensation, fever, abdominal disease, fainting, dysentery, piercing pain, cholera, leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption,
epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, vitacchikā, bilious hemorrhage, diabetes, swellings, and pustules.

Fistula-in-ano; ailments arising from bile, ailments arising from phlegm, ailments arising from wind, ailments arising from a combination of humors, ailments born of seasonal changes, ailments born of improper conduct, ailments caused by external trauma, ailments born of the ripening of karma;
cold, heat, hunger, thirst, excrement, urine, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping reptiles.
Suffering is the death of a mother, suffering is the death of a father, suffering is the death of a brother, suffering is the death of a sister, suffering is the death of a son,
suffering is the death of a daughter, suffering is misfortune regarding relatives, suffering is misfortune regarding illness,
suffering is misfortune regarding wealth, suffering is misfortune regarding virtue, and suffering is misfortune regarding view.
Of those phenomena whose initial origination is discerned, and whose cessation is discerned through their passing away;
wherein result is dependent on karma, and karma is dependent on result; wherein form is dependent on name, and name is dependent on form;
which is followed by birth, permeated by aging, overcome by sickness, struck down by death, and established in suffering.
Without protection, without shelter, without refuge, and having become without refuge—these are called sufferings.
From where have these sufferings arisen?
From where are they born? From where are they produced? From where do they come into being? From where are they fully manifested?
"From where have they appeared? What is their source, what is their origin, what is their birth, and what is their provenance?"—thus he asks about the root of these sufferings;

he asks for the cause, he asks for the source, he asks for the arising, he asks for the provenance, he asks for the origination, he asks for the nutriment, he asks for the object, he asks for the condition, and he asks for the origin.
He asks, he requests, he entreats, he propitiates:
"From where indeed have these arisen, which are of many forms in the world? Thus he asks about suffering.
"Whoever there may be"—this expression "whoever there may be" is a term signifying everything in every way, all in every manner, without remainder, without exception, and exhaustively.
"In the world": in the world of the states of misery, the world of humans, the world of devas, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases.
"Of many forms" means manifold, of various kinds, and diverse sufferings—
whatever [sufferings] there are of many forms in the world.
Therefore that brahmin said:
“I ask you, Blessed One, tell me this:
(said the Venerable Mettagū) I consider you one who has attained knowledge and developed the self.”
“From where indeed have these various forms of suffering in the world arisen?
“You are asking me about the origin of suffering.”
(Mettagū, said the Blessed One:
I shall explain that to you according to my understanding:
from the cause of acquisitions (upadhi), sufferings arise.
"Whatever various forms there are in the world—of these you have indeed asked me the source of suffering. "Of suffering" means:
of the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, and the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
"You ask about the origin" means: you ask about the root of suffering; you ask about the cause; you ask about the source;
you ask about the arising; you ask about the provenance; you ask about the origination; you ask about the nutriment; you ask about the object;
you ask about the condition; you ask about the origin; you entreat, you beseech, and you inspire confidence.
"You are indeed asking me about the origin of suffering.
Thus the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name, "Mettagū.
"Blessed One" (bhagavā) is a term of reverence... [as above] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely, "the Blessed One."
"Mettagū," said the Blessed One, "I shall explain that to you, just as it is understood.
That, I shall explain as the root of suffering; I shall explain it as the cause, I shall explain it as the source, I shall explain it as the origin."
"I shall declare its origin; I shall declare its source; I shall declare its nutriment; I shall declare its object;
I shall declare its condition; I shall declare its arising. I shall explain it, teach it, describe it, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, make it plain, and manifest it."
I shall explain that to you: how they understand, and how one who understands, comprehends, discerns, penetrates,
and pierces through— neither by oral tradition, nor by legends, nor by mere conjecture, nor by the authority of scriptures, nor by logical reasoning, nor by inferential grounds.

"I shall speak of that Dhamma which has been directly known by myself, realized through my own higher knowledge, and not [merely] through reflection on modes, nor through acceptance based on views or meditative contemplation—
that I will declare to you according to how I have understood it:
'Sufferings arise with acquisition as their source.'"
"Bases" refers to ten bases:
the base of craving, the base of views, the base of defilements, the base of kamma, the base of misconduct, the base of nutriment, the base of resistance,
the four acquired elements as bases, the six internal sense-bases as bases, and the six bodies of consciousness.
Bases (*upadhī*): all suffering is a base in the sense of being a source of suffering.
These are called the ten bases.

"Suffering" refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, and the suffering pertaining to hell... [and so forth].
The ruin of views is suffering.
For those phenomena whose initial origination is discerned, their cessation through disappearance is discerned;
there is result dependent on karma, karma dependent on result, form dependent on name, and name dependent on form; [and] with respect to birth—
It is followed by aging, permeated by decay, overcome by sickness, struck down by death, established in suffering, without protection,
without shelter, without refuge, and having become a state of no refuge—
these are called sufferings.

"These sufferings have acquisition as their source, acquisition as their cause, acquisition as their condition; they have acquisition as their reason; they originate, come into being, arise, are produced, are generated, and manifest"—thus, "sufferings originate with acquisition as their source.
"Whatever various forms there are in the world."
"Whoever there may be" (*ye kecīti*) is a term signifying everything in every way, entirely, without remainder, and exhaustively.

"In the world" (*lokasmin ti*) refers to the world of the lower realms, the world of humans, the world of devas, the world of aggregates (*khandha*), the world of elements (*dhātu*), and the world of sense bases (*āyatana*).
"Of many kinds" means various and manifold sufferings—
whatever [sufferings] of many kinds exist in the world.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Indeed, Mettagū, you ask me about the origin of suffering;
I shall explain that to you according to how I understand it,” said the Blessed One.
“Whatever various kinds of suffering there are in the world, they all arise with acquisitions as their cause.
Indeed, it is the ignorant one who creates acquisition.
Again and again the fool encounters suffering;
therefore, one who understands should not create acquisitions,
observing that suffering originates from birth.
"He who, being ignorant, creates acquisitions.

"He who" refers to whoever—of whatever kind, as appropriate, as ordained, as categorized, in whatever state situated, and endowed with whatever qualities—he may be: whether a kshatriya, a brahmin, a vaisya, a sudra, a householder, one gone forth, a deva, or a human.
"Ignorant" means one who is enveloped in ignorance, lacking knowledge, without discernment, and of poor wisdom.

"He creates a substrate" means he creates the substrate of craving, he creates the substrate of views, he creates the substrate of defilements, he creates the substrate of kamma, he creates the substrate of misconduct,
he creates the substrate of nutriment, he creates the substrate of resistance, he creates the four clung-to elements as a substrate,
he creates the six internal sense bases as a substrate, and [he creates] the six bodies of consciousness...
"He creates acquisitions, generates them, produces them, brings them forth, and fully manifests them"—
thus the ignorant one creates acquisitions.
"The dull-witted one repeatedly encounters suffering"— he repeatedly encounters the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, and the suffering of illness.
The suffering of death, the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair comes upon him, approaches him, draws near, seizes him,
clings to him, and adheres to him;
thus he undergoes suffering again and again.
"The dullard is slow-witted, deluded, ignorant, immersed in ignorance, lacking knowledge, without discernment, and of poor wisdom—
the dullard repeatedly encounters suffering. Therefore,
one who understands should not create acquisitions."
Therefore, for that reason, by that cause, by that condition, and with that as the source—perceiving this danger regarding acquisitions (*upadhīsu*)—for that reason [it is said].

One understands; understanding, comprehending, discerning, and penetrating [the truth]: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) are impermanent," one understands, comprehends, discerns, and penetrates;
"All conditioned phenomena are suffering" ... [and so on] ...
“‘All phenomena are non-self’ …pe… ‘Whatever is subject to arising,
all that is subject to cessation’— understanding this, comprehending it, discerning it, penetrating it, and breaking through it,
one does not create a substrate; one should not create the substrate of craving, one should not create the substrate of views, nor the substrate of defilements.”

One would not create; one would not create the substrate of misconduct, one would not create the substrate of nutriment, one would not create the substrate of resistance, one would not create the four clung-to elements as a substrate, one would not create the six internal bases as a substrate, one would not create the six bodies of consciousness as a substrate;
one would not produce, one would not bring about, one would not generate, one would not cause to arise.
Therefore, one who understands should not create acquisitions.
"Of suffering" means of the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, and the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

"Contemplating the source" means contemplating the root of suffering, contemplating its cause, contemplating its origin, contemplating its arising, contemplating its source, contemplating its origination, contemplating its nutriment, contemplating its object, contemplating its condition, and contemplating its accumulation.
Contemplation is called knowledge.
It is that wisdom, understanding ... [and so on] ... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
One is endowed with this wisdom of contemplation, fully endowed, approached, fully approached, attained, fully attained, possessed, and fully possessed of it.
Thus he is called "one who contemplates":
one who contemplates the origin of birth as suffering.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The fool who, being ignorant, creates acquisitions,
repeatedly encounters suffering;
therefore, one who understands should not create acquisitions.”
“Observing the origin of suffering through birth”—this you have explained to us as we asked.
Now we ask another; please tell us that.
How indeed do the wise cross over the flood,
as well as birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation?
O Sage, please explain that well to me.
For this Dhamma is known by you.
That which we asked, he has proclaimed; that which we asked, we entreated, we requested, we inspired with confidence—he has proclaimed.
"Proclaimed" means: it has been told, fully told, declared, taught, described, established, set forth, revealed, analyzed, made plain, and manifested.
"What we asked, you have explained to us.
We ask another [question]; please, speak on that. "We ask another; we entreat another; we beseech another; we inspire confidence in another; we ask further. "Please, speak on that"—that is:
"please speak, declare, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, make plain, and elucidate."
We ask you another thing; please tell us that:
how indeed do the wise cross over the flood—birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation? "How indeed?
is a question born of doubt, a question born of perplexity, a question born of hesitation, a question of uncertainty.
“Is it thus? Is it not thus? What is it? How is it?”—this is “how indeed.
The wise ones (*dhīrā*) are those who are steadfast, learned, possessed of wisdom, endowed with intelligence, knowledgeable, discerning, and sagacious.
The floods are the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.

Birth is the birth, the being born, the descent, the manifestation, the full manifestation of beings in their respective classes of beings; it is the appearance of the aggregates and the acquisition of the sense bases.

Aging is the aging and decrepitude of those respective beings in their respective classes of beings; it is the brokenness, the graying, the wrinkling of skin, the decline of the life-span, and the maturation of the faculties.
Sorrow is the grieving, the state of grieving, of one who is touched by misfortune concerning relatives,
or touched by misfortune concerning wealth, or touched by misfortune concerning illness, or touched by misfortune concerning virtue, or touched by misfortune concerning views,
or possessed of some other kind of misfortune, or touched by some other kind of painful condition.
Sorrow is internal grief, internal anguish, internal burning, internal fever, the consuming of the mind, dejection, and the dart of sorrow.
Lamentation is the wailing of one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives, or afflicted by the loss of wealth, or afflicted by illness,
or afflicted by the loss of virtue, or afflicted by the loss of right view, or by some other such misfortune.
For one who is possessed of misfortune or touched by some kind of painful state, there is crying out, lamenting,
the act of crying out, the act of lamenting, the state of crying out, the state of lamenting, vain speech, futile speech, wailing, the act of wailing, and the state of wailing.

"How indeed do the wise cross over the flood, birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation?"—that is, how do the wise cross over, emerge from, leap across, transcend, and surmount the flood, birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation?
"How indeed do the wise cross over the flood, birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation?
Please explain this well to me, O Sage."
Therefore, whatever I ask, whatever I entreat, whatever I beseech, and whatever I propitiate—“Muni”:
here “muna” is said to be knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
It is that wisdom, understanding … [as above] … non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, and right view.
The Blessed One, endowed with that knowledge, is a sage who has attained sagehood.
There are three kinds of sagehood:
sagehood of body, sagehood of speech, and sagehood of mind.
What is bodily integrity?
The abandoning of the three kinds of bodily misconduct is bodily integrity;
the three kinds of bodily good conduct are bodily integrity.
Knowledge regarding the body as its object is bodily modesty.
Full understanding of the body is bodily modesty.
The path accompanied by full understanding is bodily modesty.
The abandoning of desire and lust for the body is bodily integrity.
The cessation of bodily formations through the attainment of the fourth jhāna is bodily integrity.
This is bodily integrity.
What is sagacity of speech?
The abandoning of the four kinds of verbal misconduct is sagacity of speech;
the four kinds of verbal good conduct are sagacity of speech.
Knowledge regarding the object of speech is verbal integrity (*vācī-moneyya*).
Thorough understanding of speech is verbal integrity.
The path accompanied by thorough understanding is verbal integrity.
The abandoning of desire and lust for speech is verbal integrity (*vācīmoneyya*).
The cessation of verbal formations through the attainment of the second jhāna is verbal integrity.
This is verbal integrity.
What is purity of mind?
The abandoning of the three kinds of mental misconduct is purity of mind;
the three kinds of mental good conduct are purity of mind.
Knowledge regarding the mental object is mental mastery.
Full understanding of the mind is mental mastery.
The path accompanied by full understanding is mental mastery.
The abandoning of desire and lust for the mind is mental purity.
The cessation of mental formations, which is the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, is mental purity.
This is mental purity.
The sage of body, the sage of speech,
the sage of mind, free from taints;
the sage endowed with sagacity—
They call him the one who has abandoned everything:
the sage in body, the sage in speech,
the sage in mind, free from taints.
"The sage who has perfected sagacity is said to have washed away his evil. Thus,
they are endowed with these three qualities of sagacity.
There are six kinds of sages:
the householder sage, the homeless sage, the trainee sage, the non-trainee sage, the paccekabuddha sage, and the sage of sages.
Who are the householder sages?
Those householders who have seen the state and understood the teaching—
these are the household sages.
Who are the homeless sages?
Those who have gone forth, who have seen the state and understood the teaching—
these are the homeless sages (muni).
The seven trainees are the sages-in-training.
The Arahants are the supreme sages.
The Paccekabuddhas are the individual sages.
The Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, are the sages of sages.
One does not become a sage through silence,
being merely dull-witted and ignorant; rather,
it is one who, like holding up a scale, [weighs all things].
Having taken up the superior choice, the wise man avoids all evils;
for that reason, he is a sage, a true muni.
He who understands both worlds is therefore called a sage (muni).
Having known the Dhamma of both the non-existent and the existent, [he is a sage].
Within and without, throughout the entire world,
he is worthy of worship by gods and humans—
he is the Sage who has transcended the net of attachments.
"Please explain it well"— that is, "explain it well, teach it, describe it, establish it, reveal it, analyze it, make it clear, and manifest it"—
"please explain that to me, O Sage.
For this Dhamma has been known by you in such a way"— that is, "for this Dhamma has been known, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and fully realized by you in such a way."
For this Dhamma is known to him. Therefore that brahmin said:
"That which we asked about, he has explained to us."
We ask you another thing; please tell us this:
How do the wise cross over the flood—birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation?
"May the Sage explain that well to me,
for this Dhamma is known to you.
"I shall proclaim the Dhamma to you."
(Mettagū, said the Blessed One:
"That which is known in this very life, not based on tradition—
having understood this, one should live mindfully."
"Cross over attachment to the world.
I shall proclaim the Dhamma to you.
"The Dhamma" means that which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it has the right meaning and the right phrasing; it is entirely complete and pure.
I shall praise, declare, teach, describe, and establish the pure holy life; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for spiritual power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path,
and both Nibbāna and the practice leading to Nibbāna.
"I shall reveal, analyze, clarify, and illuminate it"—
thus, "I will proclaim the Dhamma to you," said the Blessed One, addressing that brahmin by name as Mettagū.
"Non-conflict in the present life" (*diṭṭhe dhamme anītihā*).
"In the present life" (*diṭṭhe dhamme*) means: when the Dhamma is seen, known, weighed, scrutinized, realized, and fully manifested; [when one knows]:

"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent" …pe… "Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation"—this is "in the present life," when the Dhamma is seen, known, weighed, scrutinized, realized, and fully manifested.
In this way too I shall speak of the Dhamma visible here and now.

Or alternatively: when suffering is seen, I shall speak of suffering; when the origin is seen, I shall speak of the origin; when the path is seen, I shall speak of the path; when cessation is seen, I shall speak of cessation—in this way too I shall speak of the Dhamma visible here and now.

Alternatively, "in this very life" (*diṭṭhe dhamme*) means: "it is visible in this very life, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise"—thus, thinking "I shall speak of what is visible in this very life," it is said "in this very life.
"Not based on tradition" (*anītihana*) means: not on hearsay, not on legend, not on mere tradition, not on the authority of the scriptures, nor on a basis of logic.
"I shall speak of that Dhamma which has been directly known by myself, personally realized, not based on tradition,
not based on reasoning, not based on reflection on modes, and not based on approval through contemplation of views—
this Dhamma, seen in this very life. This is "not based on tradition" regarding the Dhamma seen in this very life.

Having understood that by which they live mindfully, having understood, weighed, scrutinized, and clarified it, having made it manifest—having understood, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," having understood, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering," ...
"all phenomena are non-self," ... and so on, ...
having understood, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest that "whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation."
"He is mindful" means he is mindful for four reasons:
when developing the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body, he is mindful...
[and so on] ...he is said to be mindful.
"Walking, walking; dwelling, dwelling; moving, moving; acting, acting; protecting, protecting;
maintaining, maintaining"—having understood this, one should walk mindfully.
"One should cross over clinging in the world": here, "clinging" (visattikā) is said to be craving (taṇhā).
Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness—this is called "clinging.
In what sense is it "clinging" (*visattikā*)?
It is clinging because it is "stuck" (*visatā*).
The craving that is expansive,
the craving that is spread out,
the craving that is uneven.
It clings, thus it is clinging;
it spreads out, thus it is clinging;
it deceives, thus it is clinging.
The craving for poison-roots is clinging;
the craving for poison-fruits is clinging;
the craving for the enjoyment of poison is clinging.
Or rather, that craving is vast with respect to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena;
with respect to clans, groups, dwellings, gains, fame, praise, pleasure, robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;

with respect to the sense-sphere realm, the fine-material realm, and the immaterial realm; and with respect to existence in the sense-sphere, existence in the fine-material realm, existence in the immaterial realm, existence in the percipient realm, and existence in the non-percipient realm.

"Visattikā" means being scattered and extended among the states that are seen, heard, sensed, and cognized— whether in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, in the one-constituent existence, in the four-constituent existence, or in the five-constituent existence, whether past, future, or present.
"In the world" refers to the world of the woeful states, the world of humans, the world of devas, the world of aggregates, the world of elements, and the world of sense bases.

"Cross over the attachment in the world": attachment in the world is "vesā"; that which is "veta" in the world is "visattikā. One should cross over it, go beyond it, leap over it, transcend it, and pass beyond it—thus, "cross over the attachment in the world.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“I shall teach you the Dhamma,
Mettagū,” said the Blessed One,
“which pertains to the present life and is not based on tradition.”
"Having understood that and practicing with mindfulness,
one crosses over attachment to the world"—
this I rejoice in.
The supreme Dhamma of the Great Seer;
having understood which, one who dwells mindful may cross over attachment to the world.
"And I rejoice in that.
"That" refers to your word, your expression, your teaching, your instruction, and what has been taught.
"I rejoice, I rejoice greatly, I delight, I rejoice after, I desire, I accept, I entreat, I aspire, I long for, I yearn, I crave"—thus it is said.
"And I rejoice in that:
'The supreme Dhamma of the Great Seer. Regarding "Great Seer" (*mahesi*):
why is the Blessed One called the Great Seer?
One who seeks, searches for, and pursues the great aggregate of virtue is a Great Seer (mahesi);
[likewise] one who [seeks] the great aggregate of concentration … and the great aggregate of wisdom … [is a Great Seer].
He is a Great Seer (mahesi) because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of liberation;
he is a Great Seer because he sought, searched for, and pursued the shattering of the great mass of darkness.
He is a Great Seer (mahesi) because he sought, searched for, and pursued the breaking apart of the great perversion;
he is a Great Seer because he sought, searched for, and pursued the extraction of the great arrow of craving;
he is a Great Seer because he sought, searched for, and pursued the untying of the great snare of views.
He is a Great Seer (mahesi) because he sought, searched for, and pursued the felling of the great banner of pride;
he is a Great Seer because he sought, searched for, and pursued the subsiding of the great formative activity (abhisaṅkhāra);
he is a Great Seer because he sought, searched for, and pursued the crossing over of the great flood.
He is a Great Seer (*mahesi*) because he sought, searched for, and pursued the laying down of the great burden;
he is a Great Seer because he sought, searched for, and pursued the cutting off of the great cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*);
he is a Great Seer because he sought, searched for, and pursued the extinguishing of the great fever.
One who seeks, searches for, and pursues the subsiding of great fever is a Great Seer (mahesi);
one who seeks, searches for, and pursues the raising of the great banner of Dhamma is a Great Seer; [one who seeks, searches for, and pursues] the great foundations of mindfulness... [and so on].
The great right endeavors… the great bases of psychic power… the great faculties…
great powers...
great factors of enlightenment...
the great Noble Eightfold Path...
He is a Great Seer (*mahesi*) because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great ultimate goal, the deathless *nibbāna*;
and because he was sought, searched for, and pursued by beings of great power:
"Where is the Buddha?"
“Where is the Blessed One?
Where is the God of Gods?
Where is the Bull among Men?”—thus [he asked] the Great Seer.
"The supreme Dhamma": the supreme Dhamma is called the deathless Nibbāna.
That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
"Supreme" means the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the preeminent, the highest, the sublime Dhamma.

The Great Seer’s supreme Dhamma—having understood it, they live mindfully, having made it known, weighed it, judged it, clarified it, and made it manifest; having made it known, weighed it, judged it, clarified it, and made it manifest that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent"; and having made it known, weighed it, judged it, clarified it, and made it manifest that "all conditioned phenomena are suffering"...
“‘All phenomena are non-self’ …pe… ‘Whatever has the nature of arising,
all that has the nature of cessation’— having made this known, having weighed it, having scrutinized it, having analyzed it, and having made it manifest.
One is mindful by way of four reasons:”
Mindfully developing the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as body,
[mindfully] regarding feelings … mind … [and mental phenomena].
Developing the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating phenomena among phenomena, he is mindful...
he is called "mindful. Walking, walking; dwelling, dwelling; acting, acting; performing, performing; protecting, protecting;
maintaining, maintaining—having understood this, one walks mindfully.
"Entanglement in the world": "entanglement" (visattikā) is a term for craving (taṇhā).
It is lust, infatuation, covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
In what sense is it "entanglement"? ... It is called entanglement because it is spread out and extended.
"In the world": in the world of the states of misery …pe… in the world of the sense-bases.

"One should cross over attachment to the world": attachment is a clinging in the world; one should mindfully cross over, go beyond, cross over completely, transcend, and pass beyond that attachment in the world—thus, "one should cross over attachment to the world."
Therefore that brahmin said:
“I rejoice in that supreme Dhamma, O Great Seer.”
“Having understood this and practicing with mindfulness,
one may cross over attachment to the world.
Whatever you perceive, be fully aware of it.
"Mettagū," said the Blessed One,
"above, below, across, and in the middle—
regarding these, abandon both delight and attachment."
"Having dispelled consciousness, one does not remain in existence.
"Whatever you clearly comprehend" means: whatever you understand, know, discern, fully discern, and penetrate—that is, whatever you clearly comprehend.
"Mettagū," the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name.
"Blessed One" (bhagavā) is a designation for reverence... [as above] ...it is a descriptive term based on realization, namely "Blessed One"—thus, "Mettagū, the Blessed One."
"Above, below, across, and in the middle":
"above" refers to the future;
"below" refers to the past.
"Across and in the middle" refers to the present.
"Above" refers to the world of the devas;
"below" refers to the world of hell.
And "across" refers to the human world.
Alternatively, "above" refers to wholesome states (dhammas);
"below" refers to unwholesome states (dhammas).
"Across and in the middle" refers to indeterminate phenomena (*avyākata-dhamma*).
"Above" refers to the formless realm (*arūpa-dhātu*);
"below" refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāma-dhātu*).
The middle is the form element (rūpadhātu).
"Above" refers to pleasant feeling (sukhā vedanā);
"below" refers to painful feeling (dukkhā vedanā).
"Across and in the middle" refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
"Above" means above the soles of the feet;
"below" means below the crown of the head.
"Horizontally and also in the middle"—
that is, above, below, horizontally, and in the middle.

"Having dispelled both delight and settling in these"— meaning that consciousness does not remain in existence regarding those things which have been explained, taught, described, established, revealed, analyzed, made plain, and disclosed.
Delight is called craving.
It is that lust, infatuation, ... [as before] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
Dwelling-place means two kinds of dwelling-places: [the physical dwelling and the mental dwelling].
The settling of craving and the settling of views.
What is the settling of craving?
Whatever is reckoned as craving... [and so on].
This is the settling of craving.
What is the settling of views? It is the twenty-based view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) …pe… [as before] … This is the settling of views.
This is the settling upon views.

"Having dispelled consciousness" means: consciousness accompanied by the formation of merit, consciousness accompanied by the formation of demerit, and consciousness accompanied by the formation of the imperturbable.

Having dispelled, having thoroughly dispelled, having pushed away, having thoroughly pushed away, having abandoned, having thoroughly abandoned, having removed, having made an end of, and having brought these to non-existence—both delight and settling, as well as consciousness accompanied by formations—one should do so.
Having dispelled both delight and attachment toward these, consciousness does not stand in existence (*bhava*).
"Existence" refers to two types of existence: [the kamma-process existence and the rebirth-process existence].
There is the existence of karma and the renewed existence consisting of rebirth-linking.
What is the existence of karma?
It is the volitional formation of merit, the volitional formation of demerit, and the volitional formation of the imperturbable.
This is kamma-existence.
What is rebirth-existence consisting of reconnection?
Rebirth consists of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This is renewed existence with rebirth-linking.
One does not stand in existence while abandoning, dispelling, bringing to an end, and causing the disappearance of delight and attachment,
as well as consciousness accompanied by volitional formations and kamma-existence, along with renewed existence with rebirth-linking, within that kamma-existence.
"One should not stand in a renewed existence with rebirth-linking; one should not stand, one should not settle"—having dispelled consciousness, one should not stand in becoming.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Whatever you are fully aware of—
above, below, across, and in between,” said the Blessed One to Mettagū.
"Having dispelled both delight and attachment toward these,
let consciousness not remain in existence.
Dwelling thus, mindful and vigilant, [one does not stand in becoming].
A bhikkhu, wandering having abandoned all things cherished,
should here and now, as a wise one, abandon birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation— indeed, suffering itself.
"Dwelling thus, mindful and diligent. "Dwelling thus" means:

one who abandons, dispels, brings to an end, and causes the disappearance of delight (*nandi*), attachment (*nivesana*), consciousness accompanied by volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhārasahagata-viññāṇa*), kamma-existence (*kammabhava*), and rebirth-linking renewed existence (*paṭisandhika-punabbhava*)—one who dwells thus.
"He is mindful" by way of four reasons:
when he develops the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body as a body... [and so on]...
he is called "mindful."

“Diligent” means one who acts with thoroughness, acts with persistence, acts with steadfastness, whose conduct is not indolent, whose desire is not abandoned, whose burden is not laid down, and who is diligent regarding wholesome states—

possessing therein the desire, the effort, the exertion, and the perseverance [thinking]: “How might I fulfill the aggregate of virtue that is unfulfilled, or how might I further support with wisdom here and there the aggregate of virtue that is already fulfilled?”
Irreversibility, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, striving, determination, application, diligence, and heedfulness regarding wholesome states:
"How shall I fulfill the aggregate of concentration...? [and so forth].
May I fulfill the aggregate of wisdom … the aggregate of liberation … or may I fulfill the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
"In each case, one should support it with wisdom"— that is, whatever desire, effort,
exertion, ardor, indefatigability, mindfulness, clear comprehension, zeal, striving, determination, application,
and heedfulness there may be regarding diligence in wholesome states.

“What desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, indefatigability, mindfulness, clear comprehension, ardor, and striving there might be such that I could fully understand suffering not yet fully understood, abandon defilements not yet abandoned, develop the path not yet developed, or realize cessation not yet realized”— this is what is meant.
“Resolute determination, application, vigilance, and heedfulness regarding wholesome states”—
dwelling thus, mindful and heedful,
the bhikkhu moves about, having abandoned all things cherished as "mine."
"Bhikkhus" means either a bhikkhu who is a virtuous worldling (*puthujjana-kalyāṇaka*) or a bhikkhu who is a trainee (*sekha*).

"Wandering" means wandering, dwelling, moving about, conducting oneself, maintaining, sustaining, and keeping oneself going. "Possessiveness" (*mamatta*) means two kinds of possessiveness: [possessiveness regarding the self and possessiveness regarding what belongs to the self].
The intoxication of craving and the intoxication of views … [as before] … this is the intoxication of craving … [as before] … this is the intoxication of views …

"Having abandoned intoxication with craving, having relinquished intoxication with views, having abandoned, cast off, relinquished, dispelled, brought to an end, and rendered non-existent all forms of 'mine-ness'—
thus does a bhikkhu wander, having abandoned things cherished as 'mine.
In this very life, the wise one should abandon birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation, and thus abandon suffering."
"Birth" refers to that which belongs to those various beings...
"Aging" refers to that which belongs to those various beings...
"Sorrow" refers to one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives... [and so forth].
"Lamentation" refers to one who is afflicted by the loss of relatives...
[and so on]... "Here" means in this view...
[and so on]... in this human world.
One who knows is one possessed of true knowledge, a knower, one who has discerned, one who is wise.
"Suffering" refers to the suffering of birth, and so forth, up to the suffering of grief, lamentation, and despair.
"Birth, aging, sorrow, and lamentation—the wise one should abandon suffering right here":
one who has arrived at true knowledge, who possesses wisdom, who is discerning and intelligent, should right here abandon birth and aging, sorrow and lamentation, and suffering;
he should dispel them, bring them to an end, and cause them to cease to exist.
A wise person should abandon birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation, and thus put an end to suffering right here.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Living thus, mindful and heedful..."
“A bhikkhu, wandering having abandoned things cherished,
may the wise one here and now abandon birth, old age, sorrow, and lamentation, and thus put an end to suffering.”
I rejoice in these words of the Great Sage,
so well-spoken by Gotama regarding the state beyond acquisitions;
for the Blessed One has surely abandoned suffering.
"For indeed this Dhamma is known to you.
I rejoice in these words, O Great Seer. Regarding "this":

I rejoice in, I delight in, I am glad of, I approve of, I desire, I accept, I long for, I yearn for, and I aspire to your speech, your expression, your teaching, and your instruction as it has been taught.
"Mahesi": why is the Blessed One called "Mahesi"?
Because he sought, searched for, and pursued the great aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), he is a "Great Seer" (*mahesi*)... [and so on] ...
"Where is the Bull among Men?"—"He is the Great Seer. Thus it is said.
"I rejoice in these words of the Great Seer:
'Well-expounded, Gotama, is that which is without substrate.
'Well-expounded' means well-proclaimed, well-declared, well-taught, well-defined, well-established, well-disclosed, well-analyzed, well-made plain, and well-revealed."
"Well-expounded, O Gotama, is the state free from acquisitions. Here, "acquisitions" (upadhī) are said to be the defilements, the aggregates, and volitional formations.
The abandoning of acquisition, the stilling of acquisition, the relinquishing of acquisition, the subsiding of acquisition—the deathless Nibbāna—is thus well-expounded.
"Well-expounded, O Gotama, is the state free from acquisitions.
Truly, the Blessed One has abandoned suffering.

"Truly" (*addhā*) is a categorical statement; it is a statement free from doubt, a statement free from uncertainty, a statement without duality, a statement without ambiguity, a statement of cessation, a decisive statement, and a definitive statement.
"Addhā":
this is a term of reverence for the Blessed One... [as above] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely, "the Blessed One.

"He has abandoned suffering": he has abandoned the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, and the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he has relinquished it, removed it, brought it to an end, exhausted it, and caused it to cease.
"Surely the Blessed One has abandoned suffering;
for this Dhamma has been known by him. Thus it is said: "For this Dhamma has been known, weighed, investigated, clarified, and fully manifested by him"—thus indeed has this Dhamma been known by him.
Therefore that brahmin said:
“I rejoice in these words of the Great Seer,
well-proclaimed by Gotama as being free from substrate.”
"Truly, the Blessed One has abandoned suffering,
for this Dhamma is known by you. Surely they too would abandon suffering."
O Sage, you who would exhort one who stands firm—
I pay homage to you, O Naga, having approached you;
may the Blessed One likewise exhort me so that I may stand firm.
"And they too would surely abandon suffering.
"They too" refers to khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, renunciants, gods, and humans.

"Would abandon suffering" means they would abandon the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, and the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; they would dispel it, bring it to an end, and cause it to cease to exist.
And they too would surely abandon suffering—
those whom you, O Sage, might instruct while remaining steadfast:
namely, the khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, those gone forth, devas, and humans.
The Blessed One said this:
“A sage” (muni)—“sagehood” (mona) is said to be knowledge … [as above] … having transcended the net of attachments, he is a sage.
“One should advise the unsteady” means one should advise the unsteady respectfully, one should advise them frequently, one should advise them repeatedly, one should instruct them.
“O Sage, you who would advise one who stands firm—
approaching you, I pay homage to you, O Naga.
The word “you” refers to the Blessed One.
"I pay homage" means: I pay homage with the body, or I pay homage with speech, or I pay homage with the mind;
or I pay homage by practicing in accordance with the goal, or I pay homage by practicing in accordance with the Dhamma and its sequence. I honor, I revere, I esteem, and I worship.
"Having approached" means: having approached, having drawn near, having come together, having fully assembled, I pay homage to him face-to-face.
He is called a "nāga" because the Blessed One does not commit transgressions; he is called a "nāga" because he does not go [to rebirth];
he is called a "nāga" because he does not come [back from parinibbāna].
An elephant.
How is it that the Blessed One does not commit an offense— that he is an "elephant"?
"Sin" refers to evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and conducive to future birth, aging, and death.
"He commits no sin whatsoever in the world," said the Blessed One to Sabhiya.
Having cast off all fetters and bonds,
he who is liberated does not cling anywhere;
such a one is called a "Nāga," being such as he is.
Thus, because the Blessed One does not come (āguṃ),
he is a Nāga.
How does the Blessed One not go?
The Blessed One is a Naga. He does not go astray through desire, he does not go astray through hatred, he does not go astray through delusion, he does not go astray through fear;
he does not act under the influence of lust, he does not act under the influence of hatred, nor does he act under the influence of delusion.
He goes; he does not go by way of conceit, he does not go by way of views, he does not go by way of restlessness, he does not go by way of doubt, he does not go by way of underlying tendencies;
he is not led, carried away, swept off, or dragged along by factional doctrines.
Thus, because the Blessed One does not go,
he is a *nāga*.
How is it that the Blessed One does not come?
The Naga:
by means of the path of stream-entry, those defilements that have been abandoned are not repeated, not returned to, and not revisited.
By means of the path of once-returning... [and so on].
By means of the path of non-returning...
by means of the path of arahantship, those defilements that have been abandoned are not brought back, are not returned to, and are not revisited.
Thus, because the Blessed One does not come back, he is called "Nāga."
"I pay homage to you, O Naga, having approached you.

May the Blessed One exhort me while I am present; may the Blessed One exhort me thoroughly, exhort me frequently, exhort me again and again, and instruct me"—thus, "may the Blessed One exhort me while I am present."
Therefore that brahmin said:
“Surely they too would abandon suffering,
O Sage, whom you would exhort regarding what is not established.”
"I pay homage to you, O Naga, having approached you;
may the Blessed One exhort me while I stand here.
[He who] would recognize a brahmin as one who has attained true knowledge—
One who possesses nothing and is unattached to the realm of sensual existence has surely crossed this flood;
he has reached the further shore, free from all harshness and doubt.
"One should recognize that brahmin as one who has attained true knowledge.
He is called a "brahmin" because he has banished seven things.

Speculative view of individuality has been banished; doubt has been banished; clinging to rules and observances has been banished; lust has been banished; hatred has been banished; delusion has been banished; and conceit has been banished.
"Evil, unwholesome states— corrupting, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, ripening in suffering, and resulting in birth, aging, and death in the future— have been cast out by him.
"Having cast out all evils," said the Blessed One, "O Sabhiya."
Vimala, well-composed and established in self,
having transcended saṃsāra, he is a perfected one (kevalī);
unbound and such as he is, he is called Brahmā.
"Vedagū": "Veda" is said to be the knowledge of the four paths...
[and so on] ...having surpassed all that is known (veda), he is a "vedagū.
"Abhijaññā" means: he should know, he should understand, he should discern, he should penetrate, he should pierce through.
One should recognize that brahmin as a master of the Vedas who possesses nothing and is unattached to sensual existence. "Possessing nothing" means being without the possession of lust,
the possession of hatred, the possession of delusion, the possession of conceit, the possession of views, and the possession of defilements.

The "trifles" are misconduct. One for whom these trifles have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided, being incapable of arising again and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—he is called "one who has nothing.
As for "sensual pleasures," in brief there are two kinds of sensual pleasures:
There are sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements ... [as before] ...
these are called sensual pleasures as objects ... [as before] ...
these are called sensual pleasures as defilements.
There are two kinds of existence:
kamma-existence and rebirth-existence, which is the renewed existence at the moment of conception... [etc.
...this is the rebirth-existence at the moment of conception.
"One who has nothing and is unattached to the realm of sensual existence" means: a person who has nothing, who is unattached, unclinging, unfettered,
emerged from, escaped from, liberated from, and dissociated from the realm of sensual existence, dwelling with a mind for which no boundaries remain— that is,
"one who has nothing and is unattached to the realm of sensual existence."
"Truly indeed he has crossed this flood.
"Addhā" is a term of affirmation; it is a term of certainty...
it is a term of establishment.
"Addhā" means:
the flood (ogha) refers to the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
"He crossed over" (atārī) means he went beyond, traversed, transcended, and passed over.
"Truly, he has crossed this flood.
Crossed over, having reached the further shore, free from harshness and free from longing.

Regarding "crossed over": he has crossed the flood of sensual desire, crossed the flood of existence, crossed the flood of views, and crossed the flood of ignorance; he has crossed the path of saṃsāra—having emerged, having gone beyond, having transcended, having completely surpassed, and having passed beyond it.

Thus he has completed his residence [in the training], practiced the way of conduct, reached the goal, traversed the path, and attained the limit; he has guarded the holy life, reached the supreme vision, developed the path, abandoned the defilements, penetrated the unshakable, and realized cessation.
Suffering has been fully understood by him, its origin abandoned, the path developed, and cessation realized.

That which was to be directly known has been directly known; that which was to be fully understood has been fully understood; that which was to be abandoned has been abandoned; that which was to be developed has been developed; and that which was to be realized has been realized.
Thus, with the cross-bar lifted, the trench filled in, the pillar uprooted, the gate unhinged, he is noble, with banner lowered, with burden laid down, detached,
having abandoned the five factors, endowed with the six factors, guarded by a single guard, possessing four supports, having shaken off individual truth-claims, having utterly relinquished seeking,
with untroubled intention, with the bodily formation stilled, well-liberated in mind, and well-liberated in wisdom.

The Kevalin, the one who has lived the holy life, the supreme person, the highest person, who has attained the highest attainment—he neither accumulates nor diminishes; having ceased diminishing, he stands firm.
He neither abandons nor grasps; having abandoned, he stands firm.
He neither suppresses nor emits; he stands having suppressed.
He neither fans out nor fans in; he stands having fanned out.
He stands because he is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training.
With the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training … with the aggregate of wisdom … with the aggregate of liberation …
He stands because he is endowed with the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
He stands having fully realized the truth.
He stands having transcended all agitation.
He stands having exhausted the fire of the defilements.
He stands by way of non-attachment.
How does he stand having undertaken [the training]?
He stands firm in the practice of liberation;
he stands firm in the purification of loving-kindness; [he stands firm] in compassion... [and so on].
He stands firm in the purity of sympathetic joy... in the purity of equanimity.
He stands firm in ultimate purity.
He stands firm in the purity of non-identification.
He stands firm because of liberation.
He stands firm because of contentment.
He stands at the limit of the aggregates.
He stands at the limit of the elements.
He stands at the limit of the sense bases.
He stands at the limit of wandering;
he stands at the limit of rebirth;
he stands at the limit of rebirth-linking.
He stands at the limit of existence;
he stands at the limit of saṃsāra;
he stands at the limit of the cycle of rebirth.
He stands in his final existence;
he stands in his final rebirth;
he is an Arahant bearing his final body.
“This is his final existence;
this is his last physical aggregate.
The cycle of birth and death has come to an end.”
“There is no further becoming for him.
“The one who has crossed over” refers to the further shore; the further shore is called the deathless Nibbāna.
That which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
Thus he has gone to the further shore, reached the further shore; gone to the end, reached the end; gone to the limit, reached the limit;

gone to the boundary, reached the boundary; gone to the culmination, reached the culmination; gone to the refuge, reached the refuge; gone to the shelter, reached the shelter; gone to the protection, reached the protection;
gone to fearlessness, reached fearlessness; gone to the deathless, reached the deathless; gone to the immortal, reached the immortal; gone to Nibbāna, reached Nibbāna.
Thus, having completed his residence [in the training], having practiced the course of conduct... [and so on] ...the cycle of birth and death;
for him there is no further becoming—he has crossed over to the further shore.
"Without obstruction": lust is an obstruction, hatred is an obstruction, delusion is an obstruction, anger is an obstruction, resentment is an obstruction... [and so on].
All unwholesome volitional formations are barren wastes.

One for whom these wastes have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided, being incapable of arising again and burnt away by the fire of knowledge—such a person is called "one free from barren waste.

"Free from doubt" means: doubt regarding suffering, doubt regarding the origin of suffering, doubt regarding the cessation of suffering, and doubt regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
Doubt regarding the practice, doubt regarding the past, doubt regarding the future, doubt regarding both the past and the future,
and doubt regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions— whatever such doubt is, the state of doubting, the act of doubting,
perplexity, uncertainty, vacillation, the path of duality, hesitation, the grasping of multiple sides, wavering, sliding back and forth, lack of penetration, and trepidation.
It is the mental remorse of the mind.
One for whom these doubts are abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—he is called "doubt-free"—thus:
"crossed over, beyond, free from harshness, and doubt-free."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“O Brahmin, one should recognize that brahmin as a master of knowledge who possesses nothing and is unattached to sensual existence.”
"Truly, he has crossed over this flood;
having crossed to the further shore, he is free from harshness and free from doubt.
Thus speaks the wise man who is a master of knowledge in this world.
Having relinquished this attachment to existence and non-existence,
he is free from craving, free from distress, and free from hope;
such a one has crossed over birth and old age— this I declare.
And the man who is learned and a master of the Vedas here:
"learned" means one who has attained true knowledge, a possessor of wisdom, one who has discerned the truth, and is intelligent. "Who" refers to whoever such a person may be... [and so on].
Or a human being.

"Vedagu" means that "veda" refers to the knowledge of the four paths—wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-dharmas factor of enlightenment, inquiry, insight, and right view.
By means of those knowledges, he has reached the end of birth, aging, and death; he has attained the end, reached the limit, attained the limit, and reached the boundary.
He has reached the limit, attained cessation, attained rest; he has reached refuge, attained refuge, reached shelter, attained shelter;

he has reached the island, attained the island; he has reached fearlessness, attained fearlessness; he has reached the deathless, attained the deathless; he has reached the immortality, attained the immortality;
he has reached Nibbāna, attained Nibbāna.
One who has gone to the end of the Vedas is a *vedagū*; one who has gone to the end by means of the Vedas is a *vedagū*; or, because of having known the seven things, one is a *vedagū*.
The view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) is known; doubt … [and so on] … adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) is known.
lust … hatred … delusion …
Pride is recognized by him.
Evil, unwholesome states—defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—are recognized by him.
Having thoroughly investigated all the Vedas, he...
(To Sabhiya, the Blessed One said:
"Of whatever qualities there are among recluses and brahmins,
[I am one] who has become free from passion toward all feelings."
Having transcended all knowledge, he is a "knower" (vedagū).
"A person" (naro) refers to a sentient being, a human, a youth, a man, an individual, a soul, a creature, a living being, a lord of men, or a mortal.
"In this world" (idha) means in this view... [and so forth].
"In this world of humans"—
it is the wise man here, who has attained knowledge of the Vedas,
who releases this attachment to existence after existence.
"Existence and non-existence" means in existence and non-existence: in kamma-existence and renewed existence; in kamma-existence and renewed existence, in sense-sphere existence;
in kamma-existence and sense-sphere existence, in renewed existence, in fine-material existence; in kamma-existence and fine-material existence, in renewed existence, in immaterial existence;

in kamma-existence and immaterial existence, in renewed existence, in repeated existence, in repeated destinies, in repeated births, in repeated rebirth-linkings, and in the repeated production of individuality.
"Entanglements" refers to the seven entanglements:

the entanglement of lust, the entanglement of hatred, the entanglement of delusion, the entanglement of conceit, the entanglement of views, the entanglement of defilements, and the entanglement of misconduct.
"Having released" means having relinquished them, or having released them from the entanglements.
Or else, having loosened or released them from attachment, bondage, obstruction, binding, clinging, being clung to, being hindered,
fetters, and bonds— just as they prepare, release, and dismantle a carriage, a pack-animal, a chariot, a cart,
or a bullock-cart— so too, having cast off or released those attachments.
Or else, having loosened or released the attachment, the bond, the obstruction, the fetter, the clinging, the clung-to, the entanglement, the binding, and the confinement—
one releases this attachment to existence after existence.
"Free from craving, free from distress, and free from hope, he has crossed over birth and old age"— thus I say.

"Craving" means craving for forms … [and so on] … craving for mental phenomena. One for whom this craving has been abandoned, uprooted, stilled, and calmed, rendered incapable of arising and burnt away by the fire of knowledge—such a person is called one who is free from craving, devoid of craving, who has relinquished craving, vomited out craving, released craving, abandoned craving, and renounced craving;
one who is free from passion, who has cast off passion, abandoned passion, and renounced passion.
“Free from hunger, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, he dwells with a self that has become sublime”—thus he is one whose craving has vanished. “Untroubled”:
lust is a trouble, hatred is a trouble, delusion is a trouble, anger is a trouble, resentment is a trouble... [and so on] ...all unwholesome volitional formations are troubles.
He for whom these afflictions have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and calmed, rendered incapable of arising and burnt away by the fire of knowledge—he is called "free from affliction" (*anīgha*).
"Free from longing" (*nirāsa*): "longing" (*āsā*) is said to be craving (*taṇhā*).
It is that which is lust, infatuation... [as before] ...covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.
He for whom this hope—that is, craving—has been abandoned, uprooted, stilled, and subsided, rendered incapable of arising and consumed by the fire of knowledge, is called "hopeless.
Birth is the acquisition of such-and-such beings... [and] of the sense bases.
Aging is the decrepitude of such-and-such beings... [and] the maturation of the faculties.
This is called aging.
"He who is free from craving, free from distress, and free from hope, has crossed over birth and aging"—this is what I say.
He who is free from craving, free from distress, and free from hope, has indeed crossed over, transcended, surmounted, and overcome birth, aging, and death; this is what I say.

"I declare, I teach, I describe, I establish, I reveal, I analyze, I make plain, I elucidate"—he who is thus free from craving, free from distress, and free from hope, has crossed over birth and old age; of him I say this.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The wise man who has mastered the Vedas here,
having cast off this attachment to becoming and non-becoming—
he, free from craving, untroubled, and without hope, [is liberated].”
"He has crossed over birth and old age—so I say.
At the conclusion of this verse, ... [the monk said:
"The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple."
The fourth exposition: The Questions of the Young Man Mettagū.
